content.title: Client Components Where Interaction Actually Lives
content.hook: Client Components are not “better React components.”
content.context:
They are components that need browser-side capabilities.

Common reasons include:

- state,
- event handlers,
- effects,
- browser APIs,
- interactive widgets.
goals: Master Client Components Where Interaction Actually Lives: Move interactivity toward the smallest component that needs it.

content.title: Example
Notice the boundary
content.text:
Only the menu needs the client.

The surrounding page can remain server-rendered.

content.question:
A product page contains:

- product description,
- product price,
- image,
- quantity stepper.

Which part most clearly needs client-side behavior?

feedback.correct: Correct answer: C. The quantity stepper
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: C. The quantity stepper

content.title: Overusing the client
content.text:
A common beginner reaction is:

> “I need one click, so I will add `'use client'` at the top of the entire page.”

That works in the narrow sense.

But it can expand the client boundary more than necessary.

Better:

**Move interactivity toward the smallest component that needs it.**

content.title: Composition across the boundary
content.text:
A Server Component can render a Client Component.

That lets you keep server-side work and interactive controls in the same page architecture.

content.question: Which approach shows stronger architectural judgment?

options.text: Make every route a Client Component.
Make every component a Client Component.
Keep components server-side unless they actually need client capabilities.

feedback.correct: Correct answer: C. Keep components server-side unless they actually need client capabilities.
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: C. Keep components server-side unless they actually need client capabilities.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
nextSteps: Look at one of your React features and identify the smallest component that truly needs browser interactivity.

Complete the checkpoint and explain the mechanism in your own words. A wrong first prediction is expected; the mastery signal is whether you can explain the result and handle a changed case after feedback.
